title: One coffee, please
title_target: Έναν καφέ, παρακαλώ — Eh-nahn kah-feh, pah-rah-kah-loh
goal: Order food and drink at a café or taverna, and face the biggest stumbling block of A1 Greek: a noun changes its ending as soon as it becomes the object of an action.
bekal: put masculine nouns into the object form
know that feminine and neuter nouns barely change
order with θέλω and θα ήθελα
ask for the bill and pay
order Greek coffee with the right level of sweetness

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — At the taverna
dialogs.intro: Ana and Nikos sit down at a small taverna in Psyrri. Watch what happens to **ο καφές** once it becomes the thing being ordered — and what does **not** happen to **η μπύρα** and **το νερό**.

lines.id: Good evening! What would you like?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Good evening. I'd like a coffee, please.

notes: **This is the big lesson of this unit: nouns have two outfits.** The **subject** outfit is used when the noun does the action or is being talked about: *Ο καφές είναι ζεστός.* The **object** outfit is used when the action is done to it: *Θέλω **τον καφέ**.* English does this only with pronouns (he → him); "coffee" stays "coffee" either way.

⚠️ **Very welcome news: only masculine nouns really change.** Feminine: η μπύρα → **τη** μπύρα, just the article. Neuter: το νερό → **το** νερό, no change at all. So two-thirds of Greek nouns ask practically nothing of you here.

**The masculine endings that change are easy to remember, because they all drop the -ς**: ο καφέ**ς** → τον καφέ, ο φίλο**ς** → τον φίλο, ο άντρα**ς** → τον άντρα, ο μαθητή**ς** → τον μαθητή. One letter disappears, that's all.

**Θέλω is polite, θα ήθελα is more polite.** *Θέλω έναν καφέ* is perfectly normal in Greece and doesn't sound blunt the way *I want* does in English. For something softer: *Θα ήθελα έναν καφέ* (*thah EE-theh-lah*, "I would like"). What Greeks themselves use most is the shortest form: *Έναν καφέ, παρακαλώ.*
**Τι θα πάρετε; literally "what will you take?"** — that's the waiter's standard line. If you're not ready, answer *Ένα λεπτό, παρακαλώ* — one moment, please.

**Ορίστε (*oh-REE-steh*) is the second all-purpose word after παρακαλώ.** It means "here you are" when handing something over, "yes?" when answering a call, and "sorry, what was that?" when you didn't catch what someone said — you'll use that last one a lot.
**Μάλιστα** means "certainly" or "yes" in a formal tone, used by waiters, officials, and soldiers. In ordinary chat, **εντάξει** is enough.

⚠️ **Χωριάτικη σαλάτα isn't the "Greek salad" of menus abroad.** Literally "village salad": tomato, cucumber, onion, olives, and a whole slab of feta on top — no lettuce at all. Ordering it by this name is the quickest way to show the waiter you know what you're doing.

grammars.title: The object form (αιτιατική): what changes and what doesn't
body: Compare the two columns below. What changes is in bold — and notice how little it is.
after: For "a / an", ένας changes too: **ένας** → **έναν**, **μία** → **μία** (no change), **ένα** → **ένα** (no change). Again, only the masculine.

⚠️ **The -ν of τον and την often drops** when the next word begins with a soft letter (β, γ, δ, ζ, θ, λ, μ, ν, ρ, σ, φ, χ, ψ): *τη μπύρα* but *την Αθήνα*. The rule applies to feminine; for masculine, **τον** is now recommended in full every time. When in doubt, write it in full.

grammars.title: When the object form is used
body: There are only two situations at A1, and both are easy to spot.

head: Situation
Example

rows: After a verb that takes an object

after: ⚠️ **Every Greek preposition takes the object form, no exceptions.** This makes life very simple: as soon as you see για, με, από, σε, χωρίς, μέχρι, you know exactly which outfit the next word wears.
The preposition **σε** merges with the article into **στον, στη(ν), στο** — that's for Unit 8, but you've already seen it twice in the last unit's dialogue.

blocks.title: Greek coffee has three levels of sweetness — and you have to choose
items: **σκέτος** (*SKEH-tohs*) no sugar · **μέτριος** (*MEH-tree-ohs*) one spoonful · **γλυκός** (*ghlee-KOHS*) two spoonfuls. The sugar is boiled with the coffee, so it can't be added later — the waiter's question isn't small talk.
For ordinary brewed coffee: **με γάλα** with milk, **χωρίς ζάχαρη** without sugar, **με λίγη ζάχαρη** with a little sugar.
⚠️ Don't drink the whole cup of Greek coffee. The last third is grounds, and they're meant to stay there.
**Καλή όρεξη!** (*kah-LEE OH-reh-ksee*) — "enjoy your meal". The reply is **Επίσης!** (*eh-PEE-sees*) — "you too". This pair is said every time food arrives at the table.

exercises.prompt: Change to the object form. Example: ο καφές → τον καφέ.
Fill in the blanks with the right object article: τον, τη(ν), or το.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: τον φίλο — τη μπύρα — το νερό — τον άντρα — την πόλη — τον λογαριασμό
